title: Android Auto got a lot more fun the day I told Gemini Live to stop agreeing with me
excerpt: No true crime podcast hooks me like a morning fight with Gemini
content_html:
Published Nov 25, 2026, 6:01 PM EST

If you’ve ever wondered whether an AI feature on your phone is doing anything useful, Ben Khalesi has probably asked the same question. He has covered AI and Android for Android Police since 2023, with Pixel, Galaxy, Google’s apps, and the rest of the Android ecosystem never far behind. Ben is a lifelong geek with a Bachelor of Information Technology from Macquarie University, where he majored in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and he doesn’t stop at reading about AI. He works in AI engineering and automation and even runs his own AI agents on a Raspberry Pi, so when the industry announces something new, he’s the one who wants to know how it works behind the scenes and what can be trusted.

I've started picking fights with my car on the way to work. Somehow it's made my commute a lot more interesting.

Until recently, my morning drive came with a soundtrack of unsolved murders, tech industry gossip, and whatever podcast my queue picked for me that day.

That changed when Google built Gemini Live into Android Auto. Now I choose a topic before I back out of the driveway and make Gemini argue with me about it.

Some of you are probably questioning my sanity right now, but arguing with a chatbot at 8 a.m. has become one of my favorite parts of the day. I want more people to try it.

Picking a fight with your car is easier than you'd think

Your phone already has opinions, and now your car does too

A few boxes to check first. Your phone has to run Android 11 or newer with at least 2GB of RAM. Also, Gemini has to be set as your default assistant.

After my phone connects to the car, I press the voice button and say, "Hey Google, let's talk live."

I love the thought Google put into the design here. Gemini Live pops in a small panel, so it never covers Google Maps on the infotainment screen.

Google also released Personal Intelligence for Android Auto to users over 18. Gemini can now tap into connected apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Maps.

Personal Intelligence gives Gemini more material to get weird with. When it can see your inbox, it might drag an old reservation into an argument about your spending.

Google plans to give cars with Google Built-In the same treatment in the coming months. However, if you're in the European Economic Area, the UK, or Switzerland, you're out of luck on this feature.

A good argument starts with telling Gemini how to argue

The right prompt takes the gloves off

Left alone, Gemini makes a terrible debate opponent. It's a polite people-pleaser that rambles through long, unstructured monologues that defeat the purpose of a conversation.

Now, there's a bit of a knack to getting your AI to behave the way you want. Nobody gets the phrasing right on the first try. So my main advice is to play around and see how it responds.

If you'd like a starting point, here's what I do, along with examples of how to phrase things and how not to.

Debating a topic

"Let's talk about electric cars" gets you a pleasant overview. "Take the stance that electric cars are a failure. Push back on my points one at a time" gets you an argument.

Learning a subject

"Tell me about the Roman Empire" is how you end up with a lecture. Instead, I say, "Explain the fall of Rome in two minutes, then quiz me on it."

Practicing a pitch

"Help me prepare for a meeting" is too vague to be useful. "Act as a skeptical executive. Interview me, wait for my answer, and point out flaws in my logic" puts me in the hot seat.

Gemini may bend the truth to win an argument

Keep a mental list of anything that sounds too convenient

Gemini is a statistical model predicting the next likely word from its training data, and it can be confidently wrong.

So don't think Gemini's arguments are gospel. Gemini can invent a historical event or a statistic to win a point.

Even so, the good far outweighs the bad. The arguments are fun, and not everything it tells me is made up. Plenty of it is still useful.

Arguing with a chatbot takes more brainpower than driving can spare

A podcast barely asks anything of you. With the right podcast app, the queue practically runs itself.

Debating while navigating morning traffic, all while you're building counterarguments and picking apart the AI's logic, is something else.

Driving is unpredictable. The mental map you need to get through a road and spot hazards may compete with the working memory you need to hold an argument together.

So I want you to promise me that you'll drop the argument the second traffic gets dense. If a conversation needs that much of your attention, it's a dangerous distraction, and Gemini can wait.

That said, I've already picked tomorrow's topic. I'm going to make Gemini argue that pineapple belongs on pizza, mostly because I want to see how far it'll go to defend an indefensible position.

If it pulls my takeout history into the debate, I'm probably going to lose. It's OK. I'm fine with that. Still better than another 45 minutes of nodding along to someone, then forgetting what they said.
